In addition to extensive proliferation of the ductal network and deposition of adipose tissue, which of the following structural changes occurs at the terminal ends of the ducts during this developmental phase?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Dilation of the duct ends into milk-filled lactiferous sinuses

choices.label: B
choices.text: Apoptosis and sloughing of the terminal ductal epithelium

choices.label: C
choices.text: Infiltration of the duct ends by IgA-secreting plasma cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: Formation of solid epithelial nodules at the terminal duct ends

choices.label: E
choices.text: Conversion of the duct terminals into sebaceous gland units

explanation.summary: Thelarche involves extensive ductal proliferation with the formation of solid epithelial nodules at the terminal ends of the ducts.
explanation.whyCorrect: The developmental phase of thelarche involves extensive proliferation of the ductal network and the formation of solid epithelial nodules at the terminal ends of the ducts. Estradiol also promotes adipose deposition, and progesterone, growth hormone, and prolactin play supportive roles.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Lactiferous sinuses are dilated duct segments near the nipple; milk-filled lumens occur in lactation, not at thelarche.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Epithelial apoptosis and sloughing characterize involution after weaning, the opposite of pubertal proliferation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Plasma cell infiltration with IgA secretion occurs in the TDLU connective tissue late in pregnancy, not at puberty.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sebaceous glands are part of the newborn anlage and skin; duct terminals do not convert into them at puberty.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Breast

questions.stem: A 21-year-old nulliparous woman who completed puberty at age 14 asks what changes she should expect in her breast tissue over the coming years if she does not become pregnant. Which of the following is the most accurate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The ductal network will continue proliferating each year

choices.label: B
choices.text: The tissue will remain relatively stable until the onset of pregnancy

choices.label: C
choices.text: The stroma will steadily convert to adipose tissue within a decade

choices.label: D
choices.text: The alveoli will gradually fill with milk under baseline prolactin

choices.label: E
choices.text: New solid epithelial nodules will keep forming at the duct terminals

explanation.summary: Once pubertal breast development is complete, breast tissue typically remains in a relatively stable state until the onset of pregnancy.
explanation.whyCorrect: After the pubertal developmental stage is reached, breast tissue typically remains in a relatively stable state until the onset of pregnancy. The next major structural changes occur under the synergistic hormones of pregnancy, when the duct system grows rapidly and lobules enlarge.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Extensive ductal proliferation is a feature of thelarche and pregnancy, not an ongoing yearly process in the mature breast.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Conversion of fibrous stroma primarily to adipose tissue is a postmenopausal change, not one expected in a woman in her twenties.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Milk production and filling of the alveoli occur with lactation, not in the resting nonpregnant breast.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Solid epithelial nodules form at the terminal duct ends during thelarche, which this patient has completed.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Breast

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman presents after feeling a painless lump in her right breast while showering. She reports that it moves when touched and denies nipple discharge, skin changes, or trauma. Examination reveals a 1.5-cm, rubbery, freely mobile mass. She asks anxiously whether she has cancer. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Explain that a fixed, palpable mass of this kind is diagnostic of invasive ductal carcinoma

choices.label: B
choices.text: Recommend an immediate sentinel lymph node biopsy to assess for lymphatic spread

choices.label: C
choices.text: Reassure her that the mass is likely benign, such as a fibroadenoma, and obtain an ultrasound

choices.label: D
choices.text: Advise her to stop performing breast self-examinations to avoid irritating the mass

choices.label: E
choices.text: Explain that mobile, rubbery masses in young women usually represent inflammatory carcinoma

explanation.summary: A mobile, rubbery, painless mass in a young woman is most consistent with a benign lesion such as a fibroadenoma; reassurance plus confirmatory ultrasound is appropriate.
explanation.whyCorrect: Lumps like this in young women are commonly benign fibroadenomas, which are not cancerous. Her age, the rubbery texture, and the free mobility of the mass are reassuring features, and an ultrasound is obtained to confirm. Regular self-examination is encouraged because it helps a woman know her normal breast tissue.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Invasive ductal carcinoma forms a fixed, palpable mass as neoplastic cells invade the stroma; this mass is freely mobile.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Sentinel node biopsy is used to evaluate lymphatic spread of a diagnosed cancer, not as the first step for a likely benign lump.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Regular self-examination should be encouraged, not discontinued; it is how this patient found the mass early.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Inflammatory carcinoma presents with a swollen breast and peau d'orange skin changes, not a mobile, rubbery lump.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Breast

questions.stem: A 26-year-old man undergoes testicular biopsy during an infertility evaluation. In the connective tissue between the seminiferous tubules, the pathologist identifies compact clusters of large, eosinophilic cells. The major secretory product of these cells is released in direct response to which of the following hormones?

explanation.summary: Leydig (interstitial) cells are large eosinophilic cells in clusters between the tubules that produce testosterone in response to LH.
explanation.whyCorrect: Large, eosinophilic cells forming compact clusters in the interstitium are Leydig cells. LH from the anterior pituitary acts directly on Leydig cells, and they are the main cells responsible for testosterone production.

whyWrongByChoice.A: ABP is a Sertoli cell product that binds androgens in the tubule lumen; it does not stimulate Leydig cell secretion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: FSH acts on Sertoli cells, the gamete support cells, not on Leydig cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: GnRH acts on the anterior pituitary to release LH and FSH; it does not act directly on testicular cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Testosterone is the product of Leydig cells, not the stimulus for their secretion.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Testis

questions.stem: In an animal study, a protein tracer injected into the bloodstream diffuses across the basement membrane of the seminiferous tubule and reaches the basal compartment, but it never reaches the developing spermatocytes near the lumen. Which of the following structures most likely prevented the tracer from advancing?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cytoplasmic bridges between daughter germ cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fibrous septa projecting from the tunica albuginea

choices.label: C
choices.text: Gap junctions between Sertoli cells and germ cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: The thickened tunica albuginea of the mediastinum testis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tight junctions between adjacent Sertoli cells

explanation.summary: The blood-testis barrier is formed by tight junctions between neighboring Sertoli cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: As Sertoli cells mature under FSH stimulation, they form tight junctions with neighboring Sertoli cells. These tight junctions constitute the blood-testis barrier, which separates the adluminal compartment from the systemic circulation and shields spermatocytes and spermatids from blood-borne substances.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytoplasmic bridges link daughter germ cells to synchronize their development; they are not a permeability barrier.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The septa divide the testis into lobules; they do not seal the tubule interior from the circulation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gap junctions mediate communication between Sertoli and germ cells; they permit exchange rather than block it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The mediastinum testis contains the rete testis; it is not the barrier within the seminiferous tubule wall.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Testis

questions.stem: A new drug is found to be unable to cross the blood-testis barrier after entering the circulation. Which of the following germ cell populations would be most directly exposed to this drug?

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spermatozoa awaiting release into the lumen

explanation.summary: Spermatogonia sit in the basal compartment, outside the blood-testis barrier, and are exposed to the general circulation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The blood-testis barrier divides the germ cell layers into a basal compartment and an adluminal compartment. Undifferentiated and differentiating spermatogonial stem cells lie in the basal compartment on the basement membrane, where they remain exposed to the systemic circulation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Spermatocytes undergoing meiosis reside in the adluminal compartment, protected by the barrier.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Secondary spermatocytes are adluminal and shielded from circulating substances.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Spermatids undergoing spermiogenesis lie in the protected adluminal compartment.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The most mature cells sit nearest the lumen, farthest from the circulation and behind the barrier.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Testis

questions.stem: During spermatogenesis, germ cells pass through a sequence of mitotic and meiotic divisions. Which of the following cell types directly undergoes meiosis I?

explanation.summary: The primary spermatocyte is the last diploid cell of the lineage and is the cell that carries out meiosis I.
explanation.whyCorrect: Type B spermatogonia divide mitotically to form primary spermatocytes, the last diploid (2n) stage in spermatogenesis. Completion of meiosis I by the primary spermatocyte produces two haploid secondary spermatocytes.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Secondary spermatocytes are haploid products of meiosis I; they undergo meiosis II, forming spermatids.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Spermatids are post-meiotic haploid cells that mature by spermiogenesis without further division.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Type A spermatogonia divide by mitosis, asymmetrically renewing the stem cell pool and producing type B cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Type B spermatogonia divide by mitosis to generate primary spermatocytes; they do not enter meiosis themselves.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Testis

questions.stem: Electron microscopy of maturing spermatids shows a developing enzyme-filled cap forming over the nucleus of each cell. This structure, which will later enable the sperm to penetrate the outer layers of the egg, is derived from which of the following organelles?

explanation.summary: The acrosome forms from the Golgi apparatus during spermiogenesis.
explanation.whyCorrect: During spermiogenesis, the acrosome forms from the Golgi apparatus over the nucleus. The acrosome at the sperm head contains proteolytic enzymes that allow the sperm to penetrate the outer layers of the egg at fertilization.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The centriole gives rise to the flagellum, not the acrosome.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mitochondria align around the developing midpiece to power sperm motility.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The nucleolus is not described as the source of the acrosome; the nucleus itself undergoes chromatin compaction.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Rough endoplasmic reticulum is not the origin of the acrosomal cap in spermiogenesis.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Testis

questions.stem: A research protocol selectively blocks FSH signaling in the testis. Serum testosterone remains normal, but the concentration of testosterone within the seminiferous tubule lumen falls markedly. Decreased secretion of which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Luteinizing hormone by the anterior pituitary

explanation.summary: FSH drives Sertoli cell production of androgen-binding protein, which concentrates testosterone within the tubule lumen.
explanation.whyCorrect: FSH acts on Sertoli cells and stimulates production of androgen-binding protein. ABP binds lipophilic androgens such as testosterone and makes them water soluble, allowing them to remain at high concentration in the tubule lumen, where they enhance sperm development.

whyWrongByChoice.B: GnRH acts upstream on the pituitary; the scenario blocks FSH signaling at the testis, and serum hormones are unaffected.
whyWrongByChoice.C: LH signaling to Leydig cells is intact, which is why serum testosterone remains normal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Acrosomal enzymes serve egg penetration at fertilization; they have no role in luminal androgen concentration.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Leydig cell testosterone production depends on LH, not FSH, and serum testosterone is stated to be normal.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Testis

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man elects to undergo vasectomy for contraception. The surgeon ligates and transects the ductus deferens bilaterally. Which of the following changes is most likely after this procedure?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Absence of sperm in the ejaculate

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reduced sperm production within the testes

explanation.summary: Vasectomy causes azoospermia by blocking sperm transport while leaving testicular endocrine function intact.
explanation.whyCorrect: Ligation and transection of the vas deferens prevents sperm from traveling from the epididymis to the ejaculatory ducts, producing azoospermia. Because testicular endocrine function is preserved, testosterone production, libido, erectile function, and secondary sexual characteristics are unchanged.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Leydig cell testosterone production is unaffected; the procedure interrupts only the sperm transport pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Erectile function is explicitly preserved after vasectomy because endocrine function is intact.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Secondary sexual characteristics depend on testosterone, which remains normal.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Spermatogenesis in the seminiferous tubules continues; the sperm simply cannot exit through the ductal system.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Testis

questions.stem: A couple is evaluated for infertility. The man's semen analysis shows normal sperm count, morphology, and baseline motility. In vitro testing shows that his sperm fail to remove cholesterol and glycoproteins from the sperm head, never develop hypermotility, and cannot bind the zona pellucida. A defect in which of the following processes best explains these findings?

explanation.summary: Capacitation is the final maturation step triggered in the female reproductive tract that enables zona pellucida binding.
explanation.whyCorrect: After ejaculation, cervical secretions cause sperm to undergo capacitation: removal of cholesterol and glycoproteins from the sperm head and development of hypermotility, which allow binding to the zona pellucida and fertilization. Capacitation defects cause male infertility even when the semen analysis is normal.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A meiosis II defect reduces conversion of spermatocytes to spermatids and lowers sperm count, which is normal here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Spermiation is release of spermatids from the Sertoli cell scaffold into the tubule lumen; a defect would impair sperm output, not zona binding.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Spermiogenesis defects would produce abnormal sperm structure, but morphology is normal on semen analysis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The spermatogenic cycle describes new spermatogonial groups arising every 16 days; it governs production timing, not post-ejaculatory maturation.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Testis

questions.stem: On a histologic section of the testis, a network of interconnected channels is identified within the thickened connective tissue on the posterior aspect of the organ. Which of the following is the primary function of this network?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Concentrating sperm by removing excess fluid

choices.label: C
choices.text: Producing testosterone for the tubule lumen

choices.label: D
choices.text: Secreting the nutrient-rich fluid of semen

explanation.summary: The rete testis, housed in the mediastinum testis, concentrates sperm by removing excess fluid before they enter the epididymis.
explanation.whyCorrect: The posterior thickening of the tunica albuginea is the mediastinum testis, which contains the rete testis. The rete testis acts to concentrate sperm by removing excess fluid before they move to the epididymis for storage and final maturation.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The blood-testis barrier is formed by tight junctions between Sertoli cells within the seminiferous tubules.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Testosterone is produced by Leydig cells in the interstitium between the seminiferous tubules.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The nutrient and enzyme components of semen come from the seminal vesicles, prostate, and bulbourethral glands.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sperm storage until ejaculation occurs in the epididymis, not the rete testis.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Testis

questions.stem: A 28-year-old man presents with a painless mass in his right testis. His history is notable for an undescended right testis that was never treated in childhood. The mass is most likely a tumor arising from which of the following cell types?

explanation.summary: Most testicular cancers are germ cell tumors, and untreated cryptorchidism markedly increases the risk.
explanation.whyCorrect: About 95% of testicular cancers involve germ cell tumors, which appear only after puberty and are much more likely to develop in males with untreated cryptorchidism. Early germ cells share properties with embryonic stem cells and are thought to be the origin of adult germ cell tumors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The epididymis is a duct-system structure; it is not the typical origin of testicular cancer in this setting.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The tunica albuginea is a dense connective tissue capsule and is not the common source of testicular tumors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Interstitial (Leydig) cell tumors are rare compared with germ cell tumors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sertoli cell tumors are also rare and are not linked here to cryptorchidism.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Testis

questions.stem: The testes are located outside the abdomen within the scrotum. For normal sperm production to occur, the temperature of the testes must be which of the following relative to core body temperature?

explanation.summary: Normal spermatogenesis requires a scrotal temperature 2-3 degrees C below core body temperature.
explanation.whyCorrect: The testes reside in the scrotum, outside the abdomen, where the temperature is 2-3 degrees C lower than core body temperature. This lower temperature is required for normal sperm production.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A temperature above core body temperature is not compatible with normal spermatogenesis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The required difference is a modest reduction, not a large elevation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The scrotal temperature difference is 2-3 degrees C, not 8-10 degrees C.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Core body temperature is too warm for normal sperm production, which is why the testes sit outside the abdomen.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Testis

questions.stem: A 30-year-old man is evaluated for infertility due to a very low sperm count. Serum FSH is normal. Testicular biopsy shows normal-to-increased numbers of spermatogonia and spermatocytes but very few spermatids, with marked cell breakdown at the late meiotic stage. Which of the following steps of spermatogenesis is most likely deficient?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Asymmetric division of type A spermatogonia

choices.label: B
choices.text: Conversion of spermatocytes to spermatids in meiosis II

choices.label: C
choices.text: Migration of primordial germ cells into the testes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Mitotic proliferation of type B spermatogonia

choices.label: E
choices.text: Remodeling of spermatids in the epididymis

explanation.summary: In infertile males with low sperm counts, the most common deficient stage is the conversion of spermatocytes to spermatids in the second meiotic division.
explanation.whyCorrect: Most infertile males with low sperm counts have a normal FSH level and normal or even high numbers of spermatogonia and spermatocytes, but poor conversion from spermatocyte to spermatid in the second meiotic division, with late meiotic breakdown far more severe than in fertile males. This biopsy pattern matches that defect.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A stem cell renewal defect would deplete spermatogonia, which are present in normal-to-increased numbers here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Primordial germ cell migration occurs in the embryo; failure would leave no germ cells at all in the tubules.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Impaired type B mitosis would reduce spermatocyte numbers, but spermatocytes are abundant on this biopsy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: An epididymal remodeling problem would follow normal spermatid formation, yet spermatids here are scarce.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Testis

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy is evaluated during a research study of childhood endocrine function. Low levels of circulating testosterone are detected. At this age, the majority of his testosterone is produced by which of the following?

explanation.summary: Before puberty, the adrenal gland is the major source of testosterone; the testes take over as the main site only after puberty.
explanation.whyCorrect: The testes become the main sites of testosterone production after puberty. Before puberty, the adrenal gland is the major source of testosterone, so a prepubertal boy's circulating testosterone derives mainly from the adrenal gland.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The anterior pituitary secretes LH and FSH; it does not produce testosterone.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The hypothalamus releases GnRH to drive the pituitary; it is not a testosterone source.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Leydig cells become the main testosterone producers only after puberty, when LH stimulation begins in earnest.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sertoli cells support germ cells and secrete androgen-binding protein; they do not produce testosterone.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Testis

questions.stem: A pathologist examines a section of adult testis and identifies delicate fibrous septa projecting inward from the capsule, dividing the organ into lobules. How many seminiferous tubules does each individual lobule typically contain?

explanation.summary: Septa from the tunica albuginea divide the testis into 250-400 lobules, and each lobule contains one to four seminiferous tubules.
explanation.whyCorrect: Delicate fibrous septa project from the tunica albuginea into the testis, dividing it into 250-400 lobules. Each lobule contains one to four seminiferous tubules, where sperm development occurs.

whyWrongByChoice.B: 30-80 is the length in centimeters of a single seminiferous tubule, not the number of tubules per lobule.
whyWrongByChoice.C: 42-76 is the range in days over which spermatogenesis can vary among individuals.
whyWrongByChoice.D: 250-400 is the number of lobules in the whole testis, not tubules per lobule.
whyWrongByChoice.E: 250-600 is the total length in meters of all seminiferous tubules in the adult testis.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Testis

questions.stem: A cross-section of the testis is stained with trichrome, which colors fibrous connective tissue bright blue. A thin, bright blue layer is seen surrounding the entire organ. This layer is which of the following structures?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Basement membrane of a seminiferous tubule

explanation.summary: The tunica albuginea is the thin layer of dense connective tissue surrounding the testis and stains bright blue with trichrome.
explanation.whyCorrect: The testis is surrounded by a thin layer of dense connective tissue known as the tunica albuginea. Trichrome staining turns fibrous connective tissue structures such as the tunica albuginea bright blue, so a blue-staining capsule around the whole organ identifies this layer.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The basement membrane surrounds each individual seminiferous tubule, not the entire organ.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The epididymis is a separate duct-system structure that stores maturing sperm; it is not the capsule of the testis.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The interstitium is loose connective tissue between the tubules, deep to the capsule.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The rete testis is a channel network within the mediastinum testis, not a surface layer.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Testis

questions.stem: During a microdissection study, all the seminiferous tubules from one adult human testis are carefully teased apart and measured end to end. The total combined length of the tubules is most likely within which of the following ranges?

explanation.summary: The adult human testis contains 250-600 meters of seminiferous tubules in total.
explanation.whyCorrect: A single seminiferous tubule is approximately 30-80 cm long, and with one to four tubules in each of 250-400 lobules, the adult human testis contains 250-600 meters of seminiferous tubules in total. This is why the tubules are highly convoluted and tightly packed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: 30-80 centimeters is the length of a single seminiferous tubule, not the total for the whole testis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A few meters would account for only a handful of tubules, far short of the hundreds present.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tens of meters underestimates the total; the combined length reaches hundreds of meters.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Thousands of meters overestimates the total tubule length by roughly tenfold.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Testis

questions.stem: On a histologic section of the seminiferous tubule, tall cells are identified extending like pillars from the basement membrane to the lumen. Their cytoplasmic borders are difficult to see, but each has a distinctive elongated nucleus with a central nucleolus. These cells are directly stimulated by which of the following hormones?

explanation.summary: Sertoli cells, recognized by their pillar-like shape and elongated nuclei with central nucleoli, are stimulated by FSH.
explanation.whyCorrect: The cells described are Sertoli cells: they line the seminiferous tubule, extend from the basement membrane to the lumen, and have elongated nuclei with a central nucleolus. Sertoli cells are stimulated by follicle-stimulating hormone from the anterior pituitary, fitting the pattern that FSH targets the gamete support cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Androgen-binding protein is a product of Sertoli cells, not a hormone that stimulates them.
whyWrongByChoice.C: GnRH acts on the anterior pituitary to release LH and FSH; it does not act directly on tubule cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: LH targets the steroid-producing Leydig cells in the interstitium, not the Sertoli cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Testosterone is concentrated in the lumen by ABP to support germ cell development; it is not described as the stimulus for Sertoli cells.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Testis

questions.stem: Within the seminiferous epithelium, communication among Sertoli cells and between Sertoli cells and germ cells helps coordinate the cycle of the seminiferous epithelium. This communication is mediated in part by which of the following structures?

explanation.summary: Gap junctions mediate communication among Sertoli cells and between Sertoli and germ cells, helping coordinate the seminiferous epithelial cycle.
explanation.whyCorrect: Communication among Sertoli cells and between Sertoli and germ cells is mediated in part by the formation of gap junctions, which probably helps coordinate the cycle of the seminiferous epithelium.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytoplasmic bridges link daughter germ cells to each other to synchronize their development; they do not connect Sertoli cells to germ cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Fibrous septa are connective tissue partitions that divide the testis into lobules; they play no signaling role.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The basement membrane separates the tubule from surrounding vessels; it is a boundary, not a communication channel.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tight junctions between Sertoli cells seal off the adluminal compartment to form the blood-testis barrier; their role is a barrier, not intercellular communication.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Testis

questions.stem: A 38-year-old man develops antibodies directed against his own sperm after an injury that disrupts the seminiferous tubules. Which of the following properties of developing sperm best explains why the blood-testis barrier normally must keep them hidden from the immune system?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They express unique cell-surface antigens the immune system may read as foreign

choices.label: B
choices.text: They release proteolytic enzymes that directly injure circulating immune cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: They remain in direct contact with the general circulation as they mature

choices.label: D
choices.text: They secrete testosterone, which strongly activates the immune response

choices.label: E
choices.text: They shed all of their surface proteins during chromatin compaction

explanation.summary: Sperm development produces unique cell-surface antigens, so the blood-testis barrier must prevent the immune system from identifying new sperm as foreign.
explanation.whyCorrect: Sperm development leads to unique cell surface antigens, which the immune system may interpret as invading organisms. The blood-testis barrier formed by Sertoli cell tight junctions prevents the immune system from identifying newly formed sperm as foreign; once the tubules are disrupted, these antigens are exposed and anti-sperm antibodies can form.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Acrosomal proteolytic enzymes serve to penetrate the outer layers of the egg at fertilization; they do not attack immune cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Cells in the adluminal compartment are shielded from the circulation; only the spermatogonia in the basal compartment are exposed to it.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Testosterone is produced by Leydig cells, not by developing sperm, and it is not described as an immune activator.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sperm gain new surface antigens as they develop; they do not shed all surface proteins during chromatin compaction.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Testis

questions.stem: A histology student examines a cross-section of a seminiferous tubule and wants to locate the most mature germ cells, which are ready for release into the ductular system. These cells are found in which of the following locations?

explanation.summary: Germ cell maturation is arranged centripetally: the least mature cells sit on the basement membrane and the most mature cells lie next to the lumen.
explanation.whyCorrect: Germ cell stages are arranged so that the least mature cells are next to the basement membrane and the most mature cells are near the lumen of the tubule, ready to be released into the ductular system. Sperm differentiation proceeds centripetally, from the periphery of the tubule toward the lumen.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The basement membrane is where the least mature cells, the spermatogonia, reside.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The interstitium contains Leydig cells and blood vessels, not developing germ cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The mediastinum testis houses the rete testis; germ cell maturation occurs within the tubules.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The septa are connective tissue partitions between lobules and contain no germ cells.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Testis

questions.stem: A healthy man enrolls in a study tracking the fate of newly labeled spermatogonia as they progress through spermatogenesis to become sperm. On average, approximately how long should the investigators expect this process to take?

explanation.summary: Spermatogenesis takes about 70 days on average, though it varies among individuals from 42 to 76 days.
explanation.whyCorrect: Spermatogenesis takes about 70 days on average, with substantial variability among individuals, ranging from 42 to 76 days.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A few days is far too short for the full sequence of mitosis, meiosis, and spermiogenesis.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Sixteen days is the interval at which new groups of spermatogonia arise, not the duration of the whole process.
whyWrongByChoice.D: One hundred twenty days exceeds even the upper end of the individual range of 42-76 days.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A full year is far longer than any reported duration of spermatogenesis.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Testis

questions.stem: Semen analyses performed on a healthy man at random times over several months consistently show abundant sperm, reflecting continuous rather than intermittent sperm production. Which of the following features of spermatogenesis makes this continuous output possible?

choices.label: A
choices.text: New groups of spermatogonia begin spermatogenesis about every 16 days

choices.label: B
choices.text: Each individual spermatogonium finishes the entire process within one day

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mature spermatozoa re-enter meiosis whenever the sperm count falls

choices.label: D
choices.text: Spermatids remain stored within the seminiferous tubule until they are needed

choices.label: E
choices.text: The epididymis produces additional sperm between episodes of ejaculation

explanation.summary: Continuous sperm production depends on the spermatogenic cycle: new groups of spermatogonia arise every 16 days, so multiple cohorts at different stages coexist in the same tubule.
explanation.whyCorrect: For sperm production to be continuous rather than intermittent, multiple spermatogenic processes occur simultaneously within the same seminiferous tubule, with new groups of spermatogonia arising every 16 days (the spermatogenic cycle). Each population is at a different stage, so mature sperm are always being completed somewhere.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Spermatogenesis takes about 70 days per cohort, not a single day; staggered cohorts, not speed, provide continuity.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Mature spermatozoa are terminally differentiated and do not divide or re-enter meiosis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Sperm are stored in the epididymis after leaving the tubule; spermatids are not held in reserve in the tubule.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The epididymis stores and matures sperm; it does not produce them.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Testis

questions.stem: During an inguinal operation on a healthy 5-year-old boy, a small testicular biopsy is obtained. Histology shows seminiferous tubules containing spermatogonia but no spermatocytes, spermatids, or spermatozoa. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Primordial germ cells have not yet migrated into the testes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Spermatogonial stem cells remain largely inactive until puberty

choices.label: C
choices.text: His germ cells have already completed meiosis and left the testes

choices.label: D
choices.text: Scrotal temperature is too low to permit meiosis before puberty

choices.label: E
choices.text: Leydig cells suppress meiosis by secreting androgen-binding protein

explanation.summary: Spermatogonia form in the embryo but undergo only limited mitosis and remain largely inactive until pubertal hormonal signals prompt them to resume dividing.
explanation.whyCorrect: Primordial germ cells migrate into the forming testes in the embryo and become spermatogonia, but these spermatogonial stem cells undergo only limited mitosis at the fetal stage and remain largely inactive until puberty. At puberty, hormonal signals prompt spermatogonia to resume mitosis and progress toward sperm formation, so a prepubertal testis contains spermatogonia without later stages.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Primordial germ cell migration occurs in the developing embryo; the biopsy already shows spermatogonia, proving migration happened.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Spermatogenesis has not yet started in childhood; the germ cells have not entered meiosis at all.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The lower scrotal temperature is required for normal sperm production; it does not block meiosis in childhood.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Androgen-binding protein is made by Sertoli cells and supports sperm development; it is not a Leydig product or a meiosis suppressor.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Testis

questions.stem: Unlike females, who begin life with a fixed number of oocytes that declines over time, males can produce gametes continuously throughout adult life. Which of the following features of the male germ line accounts for this difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Type A spermatogonia divide asymmetrically to renew the stem cell pool

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cytoplasmic bridges permit spermatids to keep dividing indefinitely

choices.label: C
choices.text: Primary spermatocytes revert to spermatogonia when reserves run low

choices.label: D
choices.text: Secondary spermatocytes undergo repeated rounds of the second meiotic division

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sertoli cells differentiate into replacement germ cells after puberty

explanation.summary: Asymmetric division of type A spermatogonia continually generates both new stem cells (A1) and differentiating type B cells, sustaining lifelong sperm production.
explanation.whyCorrect: The spermatogonial stem cells (type A spermatogonia) divide asymmetrically, generating new stem cells (A1) to maintain the reserve and differentiating daughter cells (type B) that progress toward sperm formation. Because the A1 spermatogonia replenish the stem cell pool throughout life, males can produce sperm continuously, whereas females lack a comparable self-renewing germ cell population.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cytoplasmic bridges synchronize development of daughter cells; spermatids are post-meiotic and do not divide at all.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Primary spermatocytes are committed to meiosis; they do not de-differentiate back into spermatogonia.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Each secondary spermatocyte completes meiosis II once, forming spermatids; the division does not repeat.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sertoli cells are support cells of the epithelium; they never transform into germ cells.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Testis

questions.stem: As type B spermatogonia proceed through their mitotic divisions, the daughter cells remain connected to one another by cytoplasmic bridges. Which of the following is the primary function of these connections?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Anchoring the dividing cells to the basement membrane

choices.label: B
choices.text: Excluding circulating toxins from the adluminal compartment

choices.label: C
choices.text: Allowing androgen-binding protein to pass between the cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Synchronizing proliferation and differentiation of the linked cells

explanation.summary: Cytoplasmic bridges keep daughter germ cells connected so that their proliferation and differentiation stay synchronized.
explanation.whyCorrect: During the mitotic divisions of type B spermatogonia, daughter cells remain linked through cytoplasmic bridges, which help synchronize their proliferation and differentiation as the cohort advances through spermatogenesis together.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Attachment to the basement membrane is a property of spermatogonia in the basal compartment, not a function of the bridges between daughter cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Protection from circulating toxins is provided by the blood-testis barrier formed by Sertoli cell tight junctions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Androgen-binding protein is secreted by Sertoli cells into the tubule lumen; it is not trafficked through germ cell bridges.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chromatin compaction is an event of spermiogenesis within each spermatid nucleus, not something initiated by cytoplasmic bridges.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Testis

questions.stem: A single primary spermatocyte completes meiosis I, and its daughter cells then complete meiosis II. How many spermatids ultimately result from that one primary spermatocyte?

explanation.summary: Each primary spermatocyte yields two secondary spermatocytes in meiosis I, which form a total of four haploid spermatids after meiosis II.
explanation.whyCorrect: Completion of meiosis I produces two haploid secondary spermatocytes from each primary spermatocyte. The secondary spermatocytes then undergo meiosis II in the testes, forming four haploid cells known as spermatids.

whyWrongByChoice.A: One would imply no productive divisions; meiosis I and II each double the cell number.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Two is the number of secondary spermatocytes after meiosis I; meiosis II doubles this again.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Three is not possible from two symmetric meiotic divisions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Eight would require an additional division beyond meiosis II, which does not occur.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Testis

questions.stem: In postpubertal males, secondary spermatocytes proceed directly through the second meiotic division within the testis. Which of the following describes what happens to meiosis II in postpubertal females, by contrast?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It is completed more rapidly than in males

choices.label: B
choices.text: It produces eight gametes from each precursor cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: It is replaced by additional mitotic divisions

choices.label: D
choices.text: It generates diploid rather than haploid cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: It is arrested rather than proceeding to completion

explanation.summary: Meiosis II is not arrested in males; secondary spermatocytes complete it in the testes, unlike the arrested meiosis II of postpubertal females.
explanation.whyCorrect: After meiosis I, the male process differs from what happens in postpubertal females: meiosis II is not arrested in males. Instead, secondary spermatocytes undergo meiosis in the testes, forming four haploid spermatids, whereas in females meiosis II is arrested rather than running to completion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The female second meiotic division is arrested, the opposite of a faster completion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Meiotic divisions do not yield eight gametes per precursor in either sex; males form four spermatids per primary spermatocyte.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Meiosis II is not swapped for mitosis in females; it is halted at an arrest point.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Meiosis produces haploid cells in both sexes; arrest does not change ploidy of the products.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Testis

questions.stem: Within the seminiferous tubule, a spermatid is transforming into a spermatozoon. Which of the following events occurs during this transformation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A final mitotic division that doubles the number of gametes

choices.label: B
choices.text: Compaction of the chromatin within the nucleus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Removal of cholesterol and glycoproteins from the head

choices.label: D
choices.text: Separation of homologous chromosomes in meiosis I

choices.label: E
choices.text: Reattachment of the cell to the basement membrane

explanation.summary: Spermiogenesis reorganizes the spermatid without any cell division: mitochondria align around the midpiece, the acrosome forms from the Golgi, the flagellum develops from the centriole, and the nucleus undergoes chromatin compaction.
explanation.whyCorrect: Spermatid maturation into a spermatozoon (spermiogenesis) involves migration and reorganization of cytoplasmic organelles: mitochondria align around the developing midpiece, the acrosome forms from the Golgi apparatus, the flagellum develops from the centriole, and the nucleus undergoes chromatin compaction. There is no cell division during this process.

whyWrongByChoice.A: There is no cell division during spermiogenesis; the divisions are finished before the spermatid stage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Removal of cholesterol and glycoproteins from the sperm head is capacitation, which occurs after ejaculation in the female reproductive tract.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Meiosis I is carried out earlier by the primary spermatocyte, not by the spermatid.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Maturing cells move toward the lumen and are released by spermiation; they do not return to the basement membrane.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Testis

questions.stem: Late in their development, spermatids break away from the Sertoli cell scaffold that has supported them and enter the lumen of the seminiferous tubule. Which of the following terms describes this release?

explanation.summary: Spermiation is the release of spermatids from their Sertoli cell scaffold into the seminiferous tubule lumen.
explanation.whyCorrect: To develop into full-fledged sperm, spermatids break away from their Sertoli cell scaffold into the lumen of the seminiferous tubule, a process called spermiation. From there they travel to the epididymis for remodeling and storage.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Capacitation is the final maturation step in the female reproductive tract, involving cholesterol removal and hypermotility.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Ejaculation is the expulsion of semen from the urethra during the sexual response, long after tubular release.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Spermiogenesis is the organelle reorganization that converts a spermatid into a spermatozoon, not its release from the epithelium.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The spermatogenic cycle refers to new groups of spermatogonia arising every 16 days.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Testis

questions.stem: After passing through the rete testis, where excess fluid is removed, sperm move next into a structure where they undergo remodeling and differentiation into mature spermatozoa and are stored until ejaculation. Which of the following is that structure?

explanation.summary: Sperm leave the rete testis for the epididymis, the site of remodeling, final maturation, and storage until ejaculation.
explanation.whyCorrect: From the rete testis, sperm move to the epididymis for storage and final maturation. There they undergo remodeling and differentiation into mature spermatozoa and lie waiting until ejaculation moves them onward through the ductus deferens.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The ductus deferens conducts sperm from the epididymis toward the urethra during ejaculation; it is not the storage and maturation site.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The ejaculatory ducts are reached only after the epididymis and ductus deferens; sperm are not stored there.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The seminal vesicles contribute supportive fluid to semen; sperm do not enter or mature within them.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The spongy urethra is the final conduit for semen leaving the body during ejaculation.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Testis

questions.stem: An experimental compound selectively abolishes the pulsatile release of GnRH from the hypothalamus in an adult male animal. Which of the following sets of changes in testicular secretion is most likely to result?

explanation.summary: Pulsatile GnRH drives anterior pituitary release of both LH and FSH, so losing GnRH reduces both Leydig cell testosterone and Sertoli cell ABP production.
explanation.whyCorrect: From puberty onward, pulsatile release of GnRH from the hypothalamus stimulates the anterior pituitary to release LH and FSH. Without GnRH, both gonadotropins fall: LH-dependent testosterone production by Leydig cells decreases, and FSH-dependent androgen-binding protein production by Sertoli cells decreases as well.

whyWrongByChoice.B: ABP production depends on FSH, which also falls when GnRH is lost; ABP would not rise.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Testosterone depends on LH, which decreases without GnRH; it would not increase.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Both gonadotropins decline without hypothalamic GnRH, so neither testicular product increases.
whyWrongByChoice.E: GnRH is the upstream driver of both LH and FSH; its loss cannot leave testicular secretion unchanged.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Testis

questions.stem: A healthy man receives a drug that blocks sympathetic nervous system activity. Which of the following steps of the male sexual response would be most directly impaired?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Capacitation of sperm within the female reproductive tract

choices.label: B
choices.text: Production of androgen-binding protein by Sertoli cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: Propulsion of semen through the spongy urethra

choices.label: D
choices.text: Secretion from the seminal vesicles during arousal

choices.label: E
choices.text: Storage of sperm within the epididymis

explanation.summary: Ejaculation is sympathetically driven: sympathetic firing contracts the ductus deferens and propels semen through the spongy urethra.
explanation.whyCorrect: In response to sexual stimulation, sympathetic nerves fire and muscles contract in the ductus deferens, moving sperm from the epididymis toward the urethra; during ejaculation, sympathetic stimulation propels semen through the spongy (penile) urethra and out of the body. Blocking sympathetic activity therefore most directly impairs the expulsion of semen.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Capacitation is triggered by cervical secretions after ejaculation and does not depend on the man's sympathetic nerves.
whyWrongByChoice.B: ABP production is driven by FSH acting on Sertoli cells, not by autonomic nerves.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Accessory gland secretion during arousal is promoted by parasympathetic stimulation, which the drug does not block.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sperm storage in the epididymis is a passive holding phase and does not require sympathetic activity.

questions.topicName: Structure and Function of the Testis

questions.stem: A newly formed sperm is released into the lumen of a seminiferous tubule. Which of the following sequences correctly traces its path from that point until it exits the body?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Epididymis, then rete testis, then ductus deferens, then urethra

choices.label: B
choices.text: Rete testis, then ductus deferens, then epididymis, then urethra

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rete testis, then epididymis, then ductus deferens, then urethra

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ductus deferens, then rete testis, then epididymis, then urethra

choices.label: E
choices.text: Epididymis, then ductus deferens, then rete testis, then urethra

explanation.summary: Sperm travel from the seminiferous tubules to the rete testis, then to the epididymis for storage, then through the ductus deferens to the urethra during ejaculation.
explanation.whyCorrect: From the seminiferous tubules, sperm travel to the rete testis, which concentrates them by removing excess fluid, then to the epididymis for storage and final maturation. During ejaculation, muscular contractions move them through the ductus deferens toward the urethra, where they mix with accessory gland fluids and are expelled.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The rete testis comes before the epididymis; sperm are concentrated in the rete testis before storage.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The epididymis precedes the ductus deferens; vasectomy works precisely because the ductus deferens carries sperm leaving the epididymis.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The ductus deferens is the last conduit before the urethra, not the first structure after the tubule.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Sperm reach the epididymis only after passing through the rete testis, and the rete testis is never downstream of the ductus deferens.

questions.stem: Sperm from an infertile man show normal count, morphology, and baseline motility, but they fail to undergo capacitation when exposed to cervical secretions in vitro. Which of the following intracellular events would most likely be absent in these sperm?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Alignment of mitochondria around the developing midpiece

choices.label: B
choices.text: Compaction of the chromatin within the nucleus

choices.label: C
choices.text: Formation of the acrosome from the Golgi apparatus

choices.label: D
choices.text: A rise in cAMP with activation of protein kinase A

choices.label: E
choices.text: Formation of tight junctions with neighboring cells

explanation.summary: Capacitation depends on intracellular signaling, including increased cAMP/PKA activity, CFTR activity, cholesterol efflux, and activation of ion channels; these fail in capacitation defects.
explanation.whyCorrect: In capacitation defects, sperm may be unable to increase membrane fluidity through cholesterol efflux, activate essential ion channels for calcium, sodium, and bicarbonate, or trigger key signaling pathways, including increased cAMP/PKA and CFTR activity. A sperm that fails to capacitate would therefore lack the rise in cAMP with protein kinase A activation that normally accompanies this final maturation step.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Mitochondrial alignment around the midpiece occurs during spermiogenesis in the testis and is already complete; the man's sperm have normal morphology and motility.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Chromatin compaction is a spermiogenesis event finished long before the sperm reaches the female tract.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The acrosome forms from the Golgi during spermiogenesis; normal morphology indicates this step succeeded.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tight junctions belong to Sertoli cells forming the blood-testis barrier; sperm do not form them during capacitation.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old man and his 38-year-old partner have been unable to conceive. He fathered children in his 30s and has no history of genital surgery or infection. Which of the following is the most likely contributor to reduced fertility in men of his age?

choices.label: C
choices.text: Exhaustion of the spermatogonial stem cell pool

choices.label: D
choices.text: Failure of the epididymis to store sperm

explanation.summary: Age-related declines in male fertility are more often due to erectile dysfunction than to impaired sperm production.
explanation.whyCorrect: Although sperm count, motility, and quality gradually decline with age, most males retain fertility into later adulthood. Age-related declines in male fertility are more often due to erectile dysfunction than impaired sperm production.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Spermatogenesis continues throughout adult life; it declines gradually rather than stopping.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Asymmetric divisions of type A spermatogonia replenish the stem cell pool throughout life, so the reserve is not exhausted.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Epididymal storage is not described as failing with age; sperm continue to be stored and released.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Motility declines gradually with age but is not completely lost in most older men.

questions.stem: A 29-year-old man undergoing an infertility evaluation is found to have a very low sperm count. Which of the following additional findings would most strongly suggest that his infertility is due to impaired exit of sperm from the testes rather than impaired sperm production?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Complete absence of spermatogonia and spermatocytes on testicular biopsy

choices.label: B
choices.text: Decreased serum testosterone concentration accompanied by loss of libido

choices.label: C
choices.text: Severe breakdown of germ cells at the late meiotic stage on testicular biopsy

choices.label: D
choices.text: Normal LH, FSH, and testosterone with normal appearance and motility of the sperm present

choices.label: E
choices.text: Sperm that consistently fail to bind the zona pellucida during in vitro testing

explanation.summary: Normal hormone levels together with healthy-appearing, motile sperm indicate intact production and maturation, localizing a low count to blocked exit through the duct system.
explanation.whyCorrect: When LH, FSH, and testosterone are normal and the few sperm present have normal appearance and motility, sperm formation and endocrine function are intact. A very low count in that setting points to obstruction of the excretory duct system, such as scarring in the epididymis, blocking sperm from leaving the testes.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Absent germ cells on biopsy would indicate a failure of sperm production, not a transport problem.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Low testosterone with decreased libido points to failing testicular endocrine function, a production-side problem.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Severe late meiotic breakdown is the biopsy pattern of deficient spermatocyte-to-spermatid conversion, the most common production defect in infertile males.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Failure to bind the zona pellucida indicates a capacitation defect, which impairs fertilization without lowering the sperm count.
